runs.text: One Israeli snack. Ten times fewer peanut allergies? Here's the story. Tel Aviv. A London allergist, Gideon Lack, gives a lecture. Very few of the doctors there have ever seen a child with peanut allergy. Why? Israeli babies eat Bamba in their first year. Puffed corn, coated in peanut butter. Fun fact: Bamba launched in nineteen sixty four as a cheese snack. It flopped. Peanut butter saved it. So his team compared Jewish children in Britain and in Israel. Same heritage. Different snack. In Britain, one point eight five percent had a peanut allergy. In Israel, zero point one seven percent. About ten times fewer. Israeli babies ate a median of seven grams of peanut protein a month. British babies? Zero. That was an observation. So they ran a real trial, called LEAP: babies at high risk, fed peanut from infancy to age five. The result: up to eighty one percent fewer peanut allergies. In twenty seventeen, America flipped its advice. Peanut early, not late. And in twenty twenty four, the kids from the trial were teenagers. Still protected. Bamba isn't medicine. Ask your paediatrician before giving peanut to a baby. Did you grow up on Bamba?
